questions.prompt: What is the main requirement before tests can safely run in parallel?
options: They must be written in Java
They must be independent: no shared mutable state, no dependence on order, and their own data
They must all take the same time
questions.explanation: Parallel runs interleave tests unpredictably, so any shared state or ordering assumption causes intermittent failures.

questions.prompt: Running tests in parallel can expose bugs in the test code that never appeared in serial runs.
questions.explanation: Hidden dependencies on shared data, static fields or run order only show up when tests overlap.

questions.prompt: In TestNG, which setting runs each test method in its own thread?
questions.explanation: parallel="methods" spreads methods across threads; classes keeps a class's methods on one thread.

questions.prompt: Four workers, tests taking 10, 10, 10, 10, 40 minutes (no other bottleneck). What is the shortest possible wall-clock time?
questions.explanation: One worker must run the 40-minute test, so the run can never finish before 40 minutes; the other tests fit on the remaining workers. The longest single test bounds parallel speed-up.

questions.prompt: Parallel tests occasionally fail with 'email already registered'. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Tests share a fixed email address; generate unique data per test (e.g. append a UUID or worker id)
Parallelism must be disabled for all tests
questions.explanation: Two tests registering the same address at once collide. Unique data per test removes the shared resource.

questions.prompt: Which help isolate WebDriver sessions in parallel Java tests? Select all that apply.
options: A ThreadLocal<WebDriver> set in @BeforeMethod and removed in @AfterMethod
Creating the driver per test and passing it into page objects
A public static WebDriver field shared by all tests
Calling quit() and ThreadLocal.remove() after each test
questions.explanation: ThreadLocal or per-test drivers keep sessions separate, and remove() prevents leaks on reused pool threads. A shared static driver is the classic cause of cross-test interference.

questions.prompt: What does Selenium Grid add for parallel runs?
options: It distributes sessions across nodes with different browsers and machines, so more sessions run at once
It removes the need for waits
questions.explanation: Grid routes new-session requests to nodes with matching capabilities, increasing capacity and browser coverage. It does not speed individual tests or fix synchronisation.

questions.prompt: You move from 1 to 16 threads on one CI machine and total time drops only from 40 to 25 minutes, with more timeouts. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The machine (CPU/RAM) or a shared backend is saturated; measure resource usage, lower the thread count to what the hardware supports, or scale out across machines/shards
questions.explanation: Each browser needs CPU and memory, and the system under test has its own limits. Beyond the bottleneck, more threads add contention and timeouts instead of speed.

questions.prompt: CI splits 300 test files into 4 shards alphabetically. One shard always takes twice as long. How do you balance it?
options: Split by historical duration (e.g. greedy assignment of the longest files to the least-loaded shard)
questions.explanation: Alphabetical splitting ignores test cost. Duration-based balancing equalises shard times, so the slowest shard (the wall-clock time) shrinks.

coding.title: Balance shards by duration
coding.prompt:
Write `shard(durations, n)` where `durations` maps test file to seconds. Assign files to `n` shards using the greedy longest-first rule: sort files by duration descending (ties by name ascending) and put each into the shard with the smallest current total (ties: lowest shard index). Return a list of `n` lists of file names (each list in assignment order).

```python
shard({'a': 10, 'b': 8, 'c': 5, 'd': 4}, 2)
# [['a', 'd'], ['b', 'c']]
```
coding.starter:
def shard(durations, n):
    return [[] for _ in range(n)]
coding.solution:
def shard(durations, n):
    shards = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    totals = [0] * n
    for name in sorted(durations, key=lambda k: (-durations[k], k)):
        i = min(range(n), key=lambda j: (totals[j], j))
        shards[i].append(name)
        totals[i] += durations[name]
    return shards
coding.explanation: Placing the biggest items first, each into the least-loaded shard, is the classic LPT heuristic. It is not always optimal but gets close, and it fixes the 'one slow shard' problem that alphabetical splitting causes. Deterministic tie-breaking keeps CI shards stable between runs.
hints: Track a running total per shard.
min(range(n), key=lambda j: (totals[j], j)) finds the least-loaded shard.

coding.title: Predict the wall-clock time
coding.prompt:
Write `wall_clock(durations, workers)` that simulates a pool of `workers` pulling tests **in the given list order**: each free worker takes the next test; when all are busy, the next test goes to whichever worker frees up first. Return the time when the last test finishes. Also write `speedup(durations, workers)` returning serial time divided by wall-clock time, rounded to 2 decimals.

```python
wall_clock([10, 10, 10, 10, 40], 4)  # 50 (the 40 starts after a 10 finishes)
```
coding.explanation: A min-heap of 'time each worker becomes free' always yields the next available worker. The example shows why order matters: queuing the 40-minute test last makes the run take 50 minutes, while starting it first would take 40. Speed-up is therefore usually well below the worker count.
hints: Keep a list of the times at which each worker becomes free.
For each test, pop the earliest free time, add the duration, push it back.
The answer is the largest finish time; serial time is sum(durations).
